'''Jenő Elek Egerváry''' (April 16, 1891 – November 30, 1958) was a [[Hungarians|Hungarian]] [[mathematician]].

==Biography==
Egerváry was born in [[Debrecen]] in 1891. In 1914, he received his doctorate at the [[Eötvös Loránd University|Pázmány Péter University]] in Budapest, where he studied under the supervision of [[Lipót Fejér]]. He then worked as an assistant at the Seismological Observatory in Budapest, and since 1918 as a professor at the Superior Industrial School in Budapest. In 1938 he was appointed [[Privatdozent]] at the Pázmány Péter University in Budapest.{{sfn|Rózsa|1984}}

In 1941 he became a full professor at the [[Technical University of Budapest]], and in 1950 he was  appointed Chairman of the Scientific Council of the [[Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics|Research Institute for Applied Mathematics]] of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]].{{sfn|Horváth|2005}}

Egerváry received the [[Gyula Kőnig]] Prize in 1932 and the [[Kossuth Prize]] in 1949 and 1953.{{sfn|Horváth|2005}}

He committed suicide in 1958 because of the troubles caused to him by the communist bureaucracy.<ref name='Spedicato'>{{cite journal

==Works==
Egerváry's interests spanned the [[theory of equations|theory of algebraic equations]], [[geometry]], [[differential equation]]s, and [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix theory]].{{sfn|Rózsa|1984}}

In what later became a classic result in the field of [[combinatorial optimization]],<ref name='Schrijver'>{{cite book | last = Schrijver | first = Alexander | author-link = Alexander Schrijver | title = Combinatorial Optimization – Polyhedra and Efficiency | publisher = Springer | year = 2003 | isbn = 978-3-540-44389-6 }}</ref> Egerváry generalized [[Kőnig's theorem (graph theory)|Kőnig's theorem]] to the case of [[Graph (discrete mathematics)#Weighted graph|weighted graphs]].<ref name="Egervary1931">
{{Citation|first=Jenő|last=Egerváry|year=1931|title=Matrixok kombinatorius tulajdonságairól|language=hu|trans-title=On combinatorial properties of matrices|journal=Matematikai és Fizikai Lapok|volume=38|pages=16–28}}
</ref> This contribution was translated and published in 1955 by [[Harold W. Kuhn]],<ref name="Kuhn1955a">{{citation|first=Harold W.|last=Kuhn|year=1955|title=On combinatorial properties of matrices|journal=Logistics Papers|publisher=George Washington University|volume=11|pages=1–11}}</ref> who also showed how to apply [[Dénes Kőnig|Kőnig]]'s and Egerváry's method to solve the [[assignment problem]]; the resulting algorithm has since been known as the "[[Hungarian method]]".<ref name="Kuhn1955b">{{Citation|first=Harold W.|last=Kuhn|year=1955|title=The Hungarian Method for the assignment problem|journal=Naval Research Logistics Quarterly|volume=2|issue=1–2|pages=83–97|doi=10.1002/nav.3800020109|citeseerx=10.1.1.228.3906}}</ref> 
<!--
===Egerváry's Theorem===
Let <math>G=(V,E)</math> be a [[graph]] and let <math>w \in \mathbb{Z}^E_+</math>. A ''w-vertex cover'' is a vector <math>y \in \mathbb{Z}^V_+</math> such that <math>y_u+y_v \ge w_e</math> for every edge <math>(u,v)</math> of <math>G</math>. The ''size'' of a vector is the sum of its components.

Egerváry's Theorem can now be stated as follows. In any bipartite graph <math>G</math> with weight function <math>w:E \to \mathbb{Z}^E_+</math>, the maximum weight of a matching is equal to the minimum size of a ''w''-vertex cover. 
-->
